5053.prule: Primary stress falls on the head of the rightmost moraic trochee, feet being built right-to-left over moras: on the final syllable when it is heavy (bimoraic nucleus = long vowel or diphthong: babai 'hot', rufuː 'my village'), otherwise on the penultimate syllable (maunu 'rain', lolo 'sink', papa 'beside'; after a heavy penult the light ultima is extrametrical). A heavy syllable always receives stress; long vowels always bear word stress.
5053.srule: Secondary stress, if present, falls on the head of the second moraic trochee from the right edge of the word (feet built right-to-left over moras; a heavy syllable is a foot on its own): ˌmanuˈmanu 'something' (ma.nu)(ma.nu), ˌʔaiˈʔolu '1P.EXCL' (ʔai)(ʔo.lu). Leftward iteration beyond the second foot is not stated in 2015; Hafford 2005 §5.1 gives it ('stress iterates backwards on even-numbered syllables preceding the primary stress').

5054.dq: If a word is multi-syllabic, simply stated, stress falls on the root. Prefixes and clitics never receive primary stress. In compounds or phrases, the stress is usually on the last syllable
5054.dloc: Ch. 2 'San Francisco Ozolotepec Zapotec' (phonological sketch), §2.6 'Stress', p. 43 (of 145); vowel reduction continues p. 44 with fn. 35; tone §2.4 pp. 37-39; syllable §2.5 pp. 40-43 (ex. 17 affixed words); identity statement p. 23; phrase-level primary/secondary stress marks in elicitation frame (25) p. 53.
5054.prule: Primary stress falls on the root syllable of the word (most words are monosyllabic roots); prefixes, suffixes and clitics never carry primary stress and their vowels reduce to schwa or delete. Position is set by morphological structure (root vs. affix/clitic), not by syllable count or weight. Separate, hedged remark: in compounds or phrases stress is usually on the last syllable (i.e. the final root).
5054.srule: Not mentioned in Leander 2008, Ch. 2 §2.6 'Stress' p. 43 (§§2.4-2.7, pp. 37-45, and the elicitation frame p. 53 read): no word-level secondary stress is described.

5054.tone: Tone coexists with stress. §2.4 p. 37: 'In SFOZ, the functional load of tone is low... An initial analysis of tone reveals two phonemic tones, low (L) and high (H)... and a contour tone which I analyze as a sequence of low-high (LH), or rising'. p. 39: 'tones on unstressed tone bearing units are often realized as phonetically mid tones'; nasals and laterals are also TBUs. fn. 35 p. 44: 'Tones on unstressed affixes are also difficult to identify.' 5055.dloc: §1.1 'Faits accentuels', p. 417 (p. 3; archive.org volume p. 467); continuation p. 418 first lines; fn. 3 p. 419.
5055.prule: Fixed left-edge accent on every free morpheme/word: the accent (higher pitch + greater intensity) sits on the initial mora in words of 1-3 morae and covers the first two morae in words of 4+ morae; the accented stretch contrasts in pitch with all following syllables. In syllable terms the accent locus is always the initial syllable; the high span extends to the second syllable only when the word has 4+ morae (Lynch 2002 / Moyse-Faurie 1995: 'first two syllables' in words of more than three syllables). Not tonal; 'accent démarcatif'.
5055.srule: None: one accent per word. Rivierre 1978 §1.1 pp. 417-418 describes each free unit as an accented initial (first mora; first two morae in units of 4+ morae) followed by unaccented syllables ('L'initiale accentuée est à la fois plus intense et plus haute que le segment non accentué qui la suit... les syllabes non accentuées suivantes'); no rhythmic or secondary accent inside the word is described (§1, pp. 417-427 read). Restated by Lionnet 2025 §3.1: 'culminative (there may only be one per word)'.

5055.tone: Rivierre p. 416: the language is non-tonal ('parmi les langues non tonales de l'archipel'); register is not distinctive; he rejects Haudricourt's 'ni tons ni accents' (fn. 2). Lionnet 2025 (held draft, lingbuzz 008033, §3.1 p. 9) reanalyses the accent as a pitch drop after the first mora (<4 morae) or second mora (4+ morae): culminative, obligatory, demarcative, fully predictable.

5056.prule: SIL tradition (McLeod & Mitchell 1977; Hall 1979 after Burgess ms.): stress predictable and non-contrastive; in words with only short vowels the final syllable is stressed with alternating stresses leftward (2σ final; 3σ 1st+last; 4σ 2nd+last); long syllables (long vowel, V+i, closed) are always stressed; the final syllable of every locução is stressed; diminutive -re never stressed. 5056.srule: SIL account: additional stresses on alternate syllables counted leftward from the final (main) stress -- all-short-vowel words 3σ 1st+3rd, 4σ 2nd+4th (McLeod & Mitchell 1977) = Hall 1979:15 'na última sílaba de frases e nas sílabas alternadas que precedem' -- and on every long/closed syllable (with free variation of the short-syllable stresses when heavies are present, Hall). conflict.would_settle: Substantively the clash is final(+weight) vs penult(quantity-insensitive); what is unknown is whether both are true of different speech communities/eras. Side 1 rests on 1958-70s SIL fieldwork with near-monolingual (mostly female) speakers of the Culuene dialect area; side 2 on 1980s-2000s speakers of T.I. São Marcos (Lachnitt, Pickering) and Pimentel Barbosa (Quintino), and both modern authors themselves invoke the 50-year gap / Portuguese bilingualism (Quintino 2012:164 fn.26; Pickering 2010:238). It would be settled by (a) the unread primary analysis Burgess 1967 'Length and Stress in Xavante' ms. (SIL Brazil archive / Museu Nacional; bibliography row 12, access unknown) to see whether SIL's 'final' is word stress or the phrase-final boundary prominence that Hall calls 'o acento mais forte' and Pickering equates with Fox's level-2 accent; (b) the unread Salesian grammar Lachnitt 1988 Damreme'uwaimramidzé (bibliography row 11, print only) for a fuller independent rule; and decisively (c) an instrumental study of all-light di- and trisyllables in phrase-medial vs phrase-final and emphatic vs neutral contexts with present-day Culuene (Parabubure) and São Marcos/Pimentel Barbosa speakers, since SIL itself records emphatic lengthening of the penult of a locução and phrase-final penult lengthening in some stems (Aspectos 'Duração enfática'; Pequeno dicionário Apêndice V), which could make one set of facts yield both descriptions.

5057.dq: 満洲語は強さアクセント（ストレス、強勢）を持っている。満洲語の強勢音節は、話し手がより多くのエネルギーを使って発しており、発音が長く、強度が高い。 (§2 p. 153) ... 表 3：語の強勢の位置の違い (§5 p. 163) ... チャプチャルのシベ方言の複合語 coqu yixe [ˈʈ͡ʂʰɔqʷʰ ˈjɪx]「鶏と鴨」では、coqu の部分と yixe の部分のどちらにも強勢があり、それぞれの 1 音節目にある。この複合語における「鴨」の強勢は 1 音節目にある。しかし「鴨」が単独で使われる場合、強勢が 2 音節目に来る（yixé [jɪˈɣɜː]）。 (fn. 10, p. 156)

Word-stress definition §2 p. 153; low-pitch stress §4 pp. 157-162; distinctiveness §5 p. 163; conclusion §7 p. 164.
5057.prule: Stress position is lexically contrastive in polysyllables ending in a high-vowel phoneme (i, e, u; three of Sibe's five vowel phonemes, fn. 6): some words stress the final syllable and keep the vowel (mukú [muˈkʰuː] 'water', cixé 'flea', sisxé 'mattress', χasí 'eggplant', erdé 'morning', dexamé 'mother's sister's husband'), others stress the preceding syllable and delete the (phonologically present, fn. 8) final vowel (muku [mukʷʰ] 'dice face', cixe 'damp', sisxe 'sieve', χasi 'still', erde 'early', jirame [d͡ʑiˈɾam] 'thick'). The author gives no predictor, marks the stress with a lexical acute accent in the phonemic form, calls (13)-(17) minimal pairs by stress position, and states (§5 [2], §7, English abstract) that stress position can be distinctive in Sibe. Default for everything else (a/o/consonant-final words, and the vowel-retaining members of the i/e/u class): the high-pitch-onset stressed syllable is 'as a rule the last syllable' (原則として最後の音節; yila [jɪˈlaː], doχuluN [dɔʁʊˈlun]). The contrast is confined to final vs. penult (right-edge two-syllable window).
5057.srule: Exists, placement not given: Wang 2021 names secondary stress (第2強勢) only to exclude it from the study ('本論では第2強勢については扱っていない', fn. 14); no placement of non-primary stresses is given for Sibe words anywhere in §3.3-§4, and all Sibe transcriptions carry a single stress mark.

5058.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (the whole affixed word counts; diphthongs count as two emic syllables so that the penult rule holds); quantity-insensitive; the stressed vowel is usually lengthened as a consequence of stress. Stress is not contrastive.
5058.srule: Secondary stress falls two syllables before the primary (penultimate) stress, i.e. on the fourth syllable from the end; stated in one sentence, without an example marking it and without saying whether it iterates further left in longer words.

5062.prule: Word stress on the final syllable of the phonological word (stem + affix; one or two syllables, three only in subject-prefix + disyllabic-stem verb forms), i.e. the strong syllable of the last iambic (weak-strong) foot. 5062.quote: Within the word, the foot plays a role in Jabêm phonology. The foot is iambic, that is, in its full form it consists of a sequence of two syllables, the first weak, the second strong. Thus a two-syllable word consists of a full iambic foot. A single-syllable word has one foot but only a strong syllable, and a three-syllable word like /ka-seleŋ/ has two feet, the first (/ka/) with only a strong syllable, the second (/seleŋ/) a full foot. Word stress falls on the final syllable.

Tone is either high or low, labelled H and L in the text of this sketch. Tone also determines the voicing of stops. In an H foot any stops are voiceless; in an L foot voiced.'... 'L will be marked orthographically by a grave accent on the vowel of the strong syllable of an L foot'. 5067.dq: Ichishkiin has word level stress, with one primary stress per spoken word.
5067.dloc: Jansen 2010, ch. II sec. 2.6 'Stress', pp. 52-57; Figure 2.2 p. 56; Tables 2.10-2.11 pp. 55, 57. Hargus & Beavert 2005 secs. 3.1, 3.3, 5.3 (pp. 65-68, 87-88); Hargus & Beavert 2016 sec. 2 (p. 2) and sec. 3 (p. 3).

Note though, there are exceptions to each of these tendencies... tiichcim [tiichám] 'land, earth, country' has an unstressed long vowel.' H&B 2005 sec. 3.1: 'a greater-than-random attraction of stress to heavy syllables (-VV or -VC)'.
5067.prule: Lexical: every word has exactly one primary stress (raised pitch + greater intensity); within a root its position is unpredictable (any syllable of a root can be stressed; minimal pair pámta / pamtá) and must be learned per word. Statistical tendencies only (initial in CVCV/CVCCV roots; CVV or CVC syllables attract stress; barred-i rarely stressed), each with counterexamples.
5067.srule: None in ordinary words: 'one primary stress per spoken word' (Jansen 2010: 52); 'Words surface with one accent' (Hargus & Beavert 2014: 333); Jacobs 1931: 117 'no secondary stress' in Northwest Sahaptin. Some roots resist the stress-stealing prefixes (but not the stress-stealing suffixes) and keep the word level stress. I call these 'strong roots' following Hargus and Beavert 2006b. ... It…
5067.tone: No lexical tone. Hargus & Beavert classify Yakima Sahaptin as a pitch-accent language: H&B 2005 sec. 5.3 'pitch-accent appears to be a special case of stress... As reviewed in §3, YS appears to have all of the predicted characteristics of a pitch-accent language, including realization of accent with a predictable pitch contour'; H&B 2016 p. 2 shows Hyman's Obligatoriness and Culminativity both hold ('one and only one syllable is the most prominent'), with accented vs unaccented monosyllables ([kú] 'do' vs [ku] 'and'). Phonetic correlates: higher pitch and greater intensity, not duration (H&B 2005 sec. 4). 5068.prule: Main stress falls by default on the first syllable of the stress domain (stem plus suffixes; prefixes and phrasal clitics are outside the domain). 5072.prule: Two first-hand descriptions of the same field data disagree on the architecture. 5077.prule: No word-stress rule. Yaouré is a four-level tone language (Gadou 1992: H, MH, MB, B; Кушнир 2017: сверхвысокий, высокий, низкий, ультранизкий) with lexical and grammatical tone. The one explicit statement on stress (Кушнир 2017 §2.1.2) says stress is 'функционально не нагружено' (carries no functional load) and only that, in a foot (стопа) with more than one vowel, the second vowel is more prominent, 'что можно интерпретировать как ударение' (which can be interpreted as stress): a hedged, foot-level (sub-word) phonetic prominence, not a word-level stress rule and not a denial of stress. Consistent with §2.1.4 (p. 880): 'В структурах типа CVLV обычно происходит редукция первого гласного, порой до полного его исчезновения, особенно в быстрой речи' (the first vowel of a CVLV foot is usually reduced, sometimes to zero, especially in fast speech). Nothing is stated for words of several feet (a word is at least one foot, §2.5.0 p. 894).

5077.tone: Four level tonemes. Gadou 1992: H/MH/MB/B (p. 23; p. 71 quadruplets klú/klu̍/klū/klù 'tortue/charognard/famille/trou', pá/pa̍/pā/pà 'essaim/grappe/cadavre/paroi', sá/sa̍/sā/sà, ká/ka̍/kā/kà; the page's own key gives the marks / | — \ for H/MH/MB/B; on the second member of each set carries the MH vertical bar); §II.4 pp. 70-87 tone schemes by syllable type and rules of spreading, raising, lowering, dissimilation, copying. Кушнир 2017 pp. 878-879: сверхвысокий/высокий/низкий/ультранизкий (a̋ á à ȁ), tone-bearing unit = the syllable (vowel) ('Носитель тона — слог (гласная)'), rising sequences predominate within the foot, a word's tone depends on the tonal context to its left ('strong'/'weak' morphemes, §2.1.3), grammatical tones in verb and pronoun paradigms, intonation functions limited, downdrift rare and non-functional. On stress: Gadou 1992 is silent ('accent' once = dialectal accents, thesis p. 20 'avec des accents variés'; 'forme tonique' = emphatic pronoun/numeral forms; 'prosodique' = the /L/ element and tone; Ch. II TOC has no accent section); Кушнир 2017 §2.1.2 is explicit: stress is functionally unloaded; the second vowel of a multi-vowel foot is more prominent, 'можно интерпретировать как ударение' (hedged). tn.translation: One observes that Yaouré has four distinctive pitch levels, that is, four (4) level tonemes: high (H), mid-high (MH), mid-low (MB) and low (B), which we represent by the four conventional signs below. ... The tonemes we have just identified are level (punctual), in the sense that only constant relative pitch carries the distinctive function. ... So, whenever we have a modulated (contour) tone, it can only be interpreted, for Yaouré, as arising from two skeletal positions.

5078.heavy: Not applicable to the default rule (explicitly quantity-insensitive: penultimate stress 'even where non-penultimate syllables have a coda consonant', p. 73). In the minority alternate trisyllabic pattern the author calls syllables with a coda consonant or a V+HV sequence 'heavy' (p. 75).
5078.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the lexical word (default rule, quantity-insensitive: coda consonants in non-penultimate syllables do not attract stress); vowel length is the main correlate; stress is non-contrastive/predictable. Not all morphemes are counted: all prefixes, proclitics and the augment allomorphs (-wa, -a, -e, -we) are 'stress-unaffecting' (ori 'hit' with -wa keeps stress on the initial /o/; gow1l-a [gÓw1lá] 'count'; monosyllabic roots keep primary stress when prefixed, e.g. t1-wul [t1wúl], m-gei [m1.N gÉi] 'I put'), while most suffixes are 'stress-affecting' and counted (applicative -ki: aga-ki [a.N gá.ki]; plural -(e)gVl) (sec. 2.4.1 p. 74; sec. 2.4.5 pp. 78-80).
5078.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables preceding the primary (penultimate) stress, i.e. every second syllable leftward from the penult (Table 2.28: [mÒ.ni.kÉ.ta] 'water snake', [sà.ra.piá.ka] 'sarapiaka vine'; no secondary in trisyllables, [îa.lá.si] 'net'); Yeri avoids stressing adjacent syllables ('rhythmic stress', fn. 38). A stress-unaffecting suffix one syllable away from the primary may also bear stress ([Óriwá], fn. 32).
5078.quote: There is a default stress rule in Yeri which places primary stress on the penultimate syllable. This stress rule is described in section 2.4.1.
